question: to the Commission Nikos Pappas (The Left) Subject:

Recent public statements by senior government officials in Greece regarding the treatment of boats carrying migrants have raised concerns about their compatibility with obligations to protect human life at sea and those seeking international protection.1 The EU is founded on respect for human dignity and human rights (Article 2 TEU). Articles 1, 2, 18 and 19 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights guarantee human dignity, the right to life, the right to asylum and the prohibition of refoulement. Furthermore, Article 78 TFEU, the new Pact on Migration and Asylum (Regulations (EU) 2024/1348, 2024/1356 and 2024/1358), the 1951 Geneva Convention, Article 98 of UNCLOS, as well as the SOLAS and SAR Conventions require the protection of human life and respect for international search and rescue obligations at sea. Accordingly: 1.
How does the Commission assess public statements by state officials that may be perceived as incompatible with the above obligations and with the principle of nonrefoulement?

What measures can the Commission take to ensure that public statements do not encourage practices that may endanger human life at sea or undermine the implementation of European immigration and refugee law?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.9.2026) The Commission does not comment on individual public statements. Member States are required to implement EU asylum and migration legislation in full compliance with EU law, including the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, the principle of nonrefoulement as enshrined in Article 19 of the Charter, and the applicable obligations under international law. The Commission contributes to the consistent implementation of the EU legal framework through dialogue with Member States, cooperation with the relevant EU agencies and, where appropriate, the provision of guidance. In Greece, such dialogue is continuous at technical and political level. When it comes to cooperation with EU agencies, the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) and the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) have significant presence in Greece and are providing assistance and guidance on the implementation of the relevant legal framework. Where there are indications that practices implemented by a Member State deviate from the applicable framework, the Commission assesses all relevant information and, where appropriate, makes use of the instruments available under the Treaties to ensure compliance with EU law.
